## The Colin de Verdière Number of Polytope Skeletons

The Colin de Verdière number μ(G) is a spectral graph invariant defined in terms of a special class of matrices associated with a graph G. Specifically, μ(G) is the maximum corank of a Schrödinger operator on G that possesses exactly one negative eigenvalue. Here, a Schrödinger operator on G is understood as a symmetric matrix whose off-diagonal pattern reflects the adjacency structure of the graph, subject to a suitable transversality (nondegeneracy) condition. This parameter has attracted considerable attention because it encodes topological properties of the graph: for instance, it is known to characterize planarity and related embeddability conditions.

A significant contribution to the theory was made by Lovász in 2001. He constructed, for the 1-skeleton of any convex 3-polytope, an explicit Colin de Verdière matrix of corank 3. In other words, given any three-dimensional convex polytope, one can exhibit a Schrödinger operator on the graph formed by its vertices and edges that satisfies all the required conditions and attains corank equal to 3. This established a clean connection between the combinatorial structure of three-dimensional polytopes and their spectral invariant.

In the present work, the authors generalize Lovász's construction to arbitrary dimensions. The key insight is a reinterpretation of Lovász's matrix: it can be understood as minus the Hessian matrix of the volume function of the polar dual polytope. Viewing the construction through this geometric lens—as a second-order variation of the dual volume—makes it possible to extend the argument beyond dimension three and to work in any dimension d.

As a direct corollary of this generalization, the authors obtain the inequality μ(G) ≥ d whenever G is the 1-skeleton of a convex d-polytope. Thus the Colin de Verdière number of a polytope graph is bounded below by the dimension of the polytope, extending Lovász's three-dimensional result to the general setting.

The crux of the proof lies in determining the signature of the relevant Hessian matrix, since the definition of μ(G) requires that the associated operator have exactly one negative eigenvalue. This spectral analysis is carried out using tools from the theory of mixed volumes. In particular, the argument relies on the second Minkowski inequality for mixed volumes, together with Bol's characterization of the case of equality in that inequality. These classical results from convex geometry provide precisely the control needed to establish that the Hessian has the correct signature, thereby confirming that the constructed matrix is a valid Colin de Verdière matrix of the desired corank.

# The Colin de Verdière Number of Polytope Graphs

## Background and Motivation

The Colin de Verdière number $\mu(G)$ is a spectral graph invariant introduced by Yves Colin de Verdière in the early 1990s. Defined in terms of the maximal corank of a certain class of Schrödinger operators associated with a graph $G$—matrices satisfying a nondegeneracy condition known as the Strong Arnold Property—this parameter is remarkable for its connection to the topological and geometric properties of graphs. Notably, $\mu(G)$ is minor-monotone, and it characterizes several important graph classes: $\mu(G) \le 1$ corresponds to disjoint paths, $\mu(G) \le 2$ to outerplanar graphs, $\mu(G) \le 3$ to planar graphs, and $\mu(G) \le 4$ to linklessly embeddable graphs.

In 2001, László Lovász provided an elegant construction demonstrating that the graph of any three-dimensional convex polytope satisfies $\mu(G) \ge 3$, consistent with the fact that polytope graphs in dimension three are planar and 3-connected (a result reflecting Steinitz's theorem). Lovász's approach was geometric, relying on nullspace representations arising from the structure of the polytope. The natural question is whether this phenomenon persists in higher dimensions: does the $1$-skeleton of a convex $d$-polytope always satisfy $\mu(G) \ge d$?

## Main Contribution

This paper answers that question affirmatively by generalizing Lovász's construction to arbitrary dimension. The central conceptual advance is a reinterpretation of the relevant Schrödinger-type matrix. Rather than treating Lovász's construction as an ad hoc geometric device, the authors recognize it as arising naturally from the **volume of the polar dual polytope**. Specifically, the matrix realizing the desired corank is shown to be **minus the Hessian matrix of the volume function** of the dual polytope, viewed as a function of the positions of the facet-defining hyperplanes (equivalently, the vertices of the primal polytope).

This identification is powerful for several reasons. First, it situates the combinatorial spectral question within the rich analytic framework of convex geometry and the theory of mixed volumes. Second, it provides a natural candidate matrix whose off-diagonal sign pattern and support match the adjacency structure of the polytope graph, as required by the definition of $\mu(G)$. Third, it reduces the problem of establishing the lower bound $\mu(G) \ge d$ to a precise analysis of the corank and signature of this Hessian.

## The Role of Minkowski's Inequality

The technical heart of the argument lies in determining the **signature** of the Hessian of the dual volume—that is, understanding how many positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues it possesses. Here the authors invoke deep results from the classical theory of mixed volumes.

The **second Minkowski inequality** for mixed volumes plays the decisive role. This inequality, a cornerstone of the Brunn–Minkowski theory, constrains the mixed volumes of convex bodies and, when translated into the language of the volume Hessian, forces the quadratic form to have exactly one positive eigenvalue with the remaining nonzero eigenvalues being negative. This precise control over the inertia of the form is exactly what is needed to guarantee that the corank is at least $d$, yielding $\mu(G) \ge d$.

Crucially, establishing that the corank achieves the required value—rather than being larger than expected—depends on a sharp understanding of when the Minkowski inequality holds with equality. This is supplied by **Bol's equality condition**, which characterizes the extremal cases of the inequality (in the relevant setting of two- and three-dimensional mixed volume relations). Bol's condition ensures that the kernel of the Hessian has exactly the anticipated dimension, and it is instrumental in verifying that the Strong Arnold Property is satisfied, so that the constructed matrix is admissible in the definition of the Colin de Verdière number.

## Conclusion

By combining the geometric reinterpretation of Lovász's matrix as the negative Hessian of the dual volume with the analytic machinery of mixed volume inequalities, the authors prove that for the $1$-skeleton $G$ of any convex $d$-polytope,
$$\mu(G) \ge d.$$
This result generalizes Lovász's three-dimensional theorem to all dimensions and reveals a striking bridge between the spectral theory of graphs and the classical Brunn–Minkowski theory of convex bodies. The proof exemplifies how deep inequalities from convex geometry—the second Minkowski inequality and Bol's characterization of its equality cases—can be harnessed to control the fine spectral invariants that govern the topology and combinatorial structure of polytope graphs.

# The Colin Davis Interpretations of Verdi

Among the great conductors of the twentieth century, Sir Colin Davis holds a special place for the depth and passion he brought to the works of Giuseppe Verdi. The British maestro, celebrated for his interpretations of Berlioz and Mozart, also demonstrated a profound understanding of the Italian operatic tradition that Verdi so magnificently embodied.

## A Meeting of Musical Minds

The connection between Colin Davis and Verdi's music was not immediately obvious. Davis built his early reputation on other repertoires, yet when he turned his attention to the great Italian composer, he revealed layers of emotional richness that critics and audiences found deeply moving. The dramatic intensity of Verdi's scores seemed to resonate with Davis's own sense of theatrical timing and orchestral color.

## The Requiem

Perhaps nowhere is this partnership more evident than in performances of Verdi's *Requiem*. The monumental work, sometimes described as Verdi's greatest opera despite being sacred music, demands both delicacy and overwhelming force. Under Davis's baton, the "Dies Irae" thundered with apocalyptic power, while the quieter passages breathed with tender humanity.

## A Lasting Legacy

The recordings and live performances left behind by Colin Davis continue to inspire new generations of listeners. His approach to Verdi reminds us that great music transcends national boundaries, and that a conductor of vision can illuminate a composer's work in ways that feel both faithful and freshly revelatory.

The pairing of Colin Davis and Verdi remains a testament to the timeless power of musical interpretation.

**Higher-dimensional Colin de Verdière matrices and spectral representations of polytopes**

**Abstract.** In 2001, Lovász showed that every Steinitz representation of a $3$-polytope gives rise to a Colin de Verdière matrix of corank $3$ for the polytope's edge graph, and, conversely, that the null space of such a matrix recovers a projective representation of the polytope on the sphere. The construction hinges on interpreting the geometric data of a convex polytope—its vertex positions, together with a self-stress supported on the edges—as a symmetric matrix that behaves like a discrete Schrödinger operator satisfying the Strong Arnold Property. We generalize this correspondence to convex $d$-polytopes for all $d \ge 3$. Starting from a full-dimensional realization of a simple (or, more generally, $\ell$-simplicial) $d$-polytope $P$, we construct a symmetric matrix $M$ indexed by the vertices of $P$ whose off-diagonal support is prescribed by the edge graph $G(P)$, whose corank equals $d$, and whose null space reproduces the vertex coordinates up to a projective transformation. We prove that $M$ has exactly one negative eigenvalue and satisfies a transversality condition generalizing the Strong Arnold Property, so that $M$ is a genuine Colin de Verdière matrix witnessing the bound $\mu(G(P)) \ge d$ for the relevant polytope classes. The key new ingredient is a higher-dimensional analogue of the self-stress used in the $3$-dimensional case, obtained from the space of affine dependencies among the facet normals; this links our matrices to the stress matrices of Cauchy–Alexandrov rigidity theory and to the second-order cone structure of the polytope's normal fan. As applications we obtain spectral characterizations of $d$-polytopality for graphs in the associated classes, new lower bounds on the Colin de Verdière parameter of polytope graphs, and a uniform framework recovering both Lovász's theorem and the classical Maxwell–Cremona correspondence as the cases $d=3$ and $d=2$. We conclude with obstructions showing that the corank of such matrices cannot in general exceed the dimension, and discuss the failure of the null-space representation for non-simple polytopes.

- $M_{ij} < 0$ whenever $ij$ is an edge of $G$,
- $M_{ij} = 0$ whenever $i\neq j$ and $ij$ is a non-edge (diagonal entries unrestricted),
- $M$ has **exactly one negative eigenvalue** (simple), and
- $M$ satisfies the **Strong Arnold Property** (a genericity/transversality condition).

The parameter is minor-monotone and famously encodes topological embeddability: $\mu(G)\le 1$ iff $G$ is a disjoint union of paths, $\mu\le 2$ iff outerplanar, $\mu\le 3$ iff planar, and $\mu\le 4$ iff linklessly embeddable.

# Abstract

We establish a novel connection between the combinatorial geometry of mixed volumes and the spectral invariant μ(G), the Colin de Verdière number of a graph G. Central to our approach is a refinement of Bol's classical equality condition for mixed volumes, which characterizes when the Alexandrov–Fenchel inequality degenerates to equality for a pair of convex bodies. We show that this degeneracy locus admits a natural interpretation in terms of the corank structure of Schrödinger operators associated to G, thereby linking the geometry of tangent cones at equality points to the maximal multiplicity condition defining μ(G).

Our main theorem constructs, for each graph G with μ(G) = k, a family of convex polytopes whose mixed volume form exhibits Bol-type equality precisely along a stratum of dimension governed by k. Conversely, we prove that the transversality (Strong Arnold Property) condition intrinsic to the definition of μ(G) corresponds to the nondegeneracy of the associated Hessian in the mixed volume expansion. This yields a geometric certificate for the minor-monotonicity of μ(G): planarity (μ ≤ 3) and linklessness (μ ≤ 4) are recovered as conditions on the rank of a mixed discriminant.

As applications, we obtain new lower bounds on μ(G) via volumetric inequalities and derive a convex-geometric proof that μ is minor-monotone. We conclude by discussing extensions to weighted mixed volumes and connections with the Lovász–Schrijver theta body, suggesting a broader correspondence between Alexandrov–Fenchel degeneracy and topological embeddability of graphs.

---

*Keywords:* mixed volumes, Alexandrov–Fenchel inequality, Bol's equality condition, Colin de Verdière number, Strong Arnold Property, spectral graph theory, convex polytopes.
